abstract: We show that preparatory input currents, or bias currents, alone can make a recurrent circuit with fixed weights write all 52 cursive letters, and words built from them. Each letter is produced by its own bias pattern, ramped in as a preparatory drive and withdrawn at a go cue; the recurrent weights and the readout never change, and the readout's weights are random, with a single global gain picked on four letters (a-d). We take the stability-optimized circuits (SOCs) of Hennequin et al. and extend them with mutual inhibition: all inhibitory neurons inhibit one another through a single shared weight (MISOC, mutual inhibition SOC). With 200 units, the pen of the SOC stays on average 1.7% of a letter width from the target over all 52 letters, and that of the MISOC 0.9% (25 random circuits; R2 = 0.996 and 0.999). The other 48 letters are learned through their bias patterns alone, without changing a single synapse, so new letters cannot disturb old ones. Letters learned one at a time chain into words in one continuous run. Mutual inhibition improves the circuit: with a shared weight of 0.5 the MISOC writes with 16-48% less error than the SOC at every network size tested (50 to 200 units), and with fifty network-derived input channels instead of one bias per neuron it keeps its advantage. Bias currents and mutual inhibition let small, fixed circuits hold a large and growing motor repertoire and switch within it without any synaptic change.
